# What I would change

## The backend

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Turing.jl gave us submodels, a choice of samplers, and the rest of
  Julia. The proof of concept exists because of it, and choosing it was
  right at the time
- Automatic differentiation is the part that decided it. For a model
  somebody acts on during an outbreak, a silently wrong gradient is not
  a footnote

::: {.callout-note}
## Eleven breaking releases in nineteen months
v0.35.5, which the paper's artefact pins, to v0.46.0. Our migration was
one rename. The cost is the tracking.
:::

| Commits, last six months | Turing.jl | DynamicPPL.jl |
|---|---:|---:|
| Human authors | 29 | 72 |
| One person | **17** | **47** |

: {tbl-colwidths="[46,27,27]"}
:::
::: {.column width="4%"}
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## From the Turing.jl documentation
"not all AD libraries in there are thoroughly tested on Turing models.
Thus, it is possible that some of them will either error ... or maybe
even silently give incorrect results"
:::

**Where this showed up in our models**

- Large simulated counts error, and vectors mixing missing and observed
  values have to be handled by hand
- Profiling through the layers is hard, because the language rewrites
  the model before it runs

::: {.callout-note}
The work is good.
:::

## What this does not do yet

::: {.callout-important}
## Nobody outside the author team has built a model with this
The title says composable models can lower barriers. Until somebody
outside tries, that is an argument rather than a result.
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**In the proof of concept**

- The component library stops at basic epidemiological patterns. No
  partial pooling, and no mapping between latent and observed states
- Changing a component's order does not update the priors that go with
  it. That stays manual
- The abstraction layers have a runtime cost. We have not measured it
  properly
:::
::: {.column width="4%"}
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
**In the claim**

- The design considerations came from the authors and have had no
  community input

::: {.callout-note}
`EpiAwareR`, Sebastian Funk's prototype R interface, ran two of the
three replications. That is the closest thing to outside use so far.
:::
:::
::::
